# The Girl Who Wanted to Be Full

Mira had been thin her whole life—not by choice, but by circumstance. Growing up in a cramped apartment with five siblings and a mother who stretched a single loaf of bread across three days, hunger had been her most constant companion. While other girls dreamed of being slender like the models in magazines, Mira dreamed of softness, of round cheeks and a belly that pressed against her dress. To her, fatness meant safety. It meant *enough*.

When she turned nineteen, she walked past a struggling restaurant called *Bruno's Bistro* with a "Help Wanted" sign in the window. The smells drifting out weren't particularly good—a bit of burnt oil, overcooked cabbage—but to Mira, they were intoxicating.

She walked inside and met Bruno, a tired man with stains on his apron.

"I'll work for free," she told him. "No wages. Just give me a small room upstairs and let me eat whatever the customers leave behind."

Bruno laughed, then realized she was serious. Business was bad. The deal seemed too good to refuse.

And so Mira began her new life. The food at Bruno's was, by all accounts, terrible—rubbery schnitzels, gluey pasta, sauces that tasted of regret. Customers picked at their meals and left most of it behind. Plate after plate came back to the kitchen barely touched, and Mira ate it all. Cold dumplings. Half-eaten steaks. Mountains of fries gone soft.

For the first time in her life, she went to bed feeling full.

The weeks turned to months. Her cheeks rounded. Her dresses tightened, then split, then were replaced with larger ones. She watched herself in the mirror with delight as her thin frame disappeared beneath soft, generous curves. She had never been so happy.

But the months turned to years, and Mira kept eating. The fuller she got, the more comforting fullness became. She moved from the upstairs room to a back storage area when she could no longer climb the stairs. Then she stopped going outside altogether—the front door had grown narrower somehow, or perhaps she had grown wider.

Bruno barely noticed at first. He had his own troubles. But eventually customers began to complain about the smell drifting from the back of the restaurant. About the strange noises. About the young woman they sometimes glimpsed through a doorway, vast and unmoving.

One by one, the customers stopped coming.

Bruno tried to help her. He really did. He called doctors who wouldn't come, ambulances that couldn't fit her through any opening. He begged her to stop eating, but by then Mira couldn't imagine being empty again. Emptiness was the enemy she had spent her whole life fleeing.

The restaurant closed on a gray Tuesday in November. Bruno, ruined and weeping, packed a single suitcase. He stood in the doorway of the back room where Mira lay among the ruins of her dream.

"I'm sorry," he said. "I should have stopped this. I should have helped you when I still could."

Mira just looked at him. She didn't feel angry. She didn't feel much of anything except the familiar, terrible comfort of fullness.

"It's not your fault," she said. "I got what I wanted."

Bruno left. The restaurant stood abandoned, its windows growing dusty, its sign fading in the rain. And inside, in the dim back room, Mira lay alone with her thoughts—finally understanding, too late, that what she had been hungry for all along was never food at all.

It was the feeling of being cared for. Of being chosen. Of mattering to someone.

And that was a hunger no plate could ever fill.

---

*A cautionary tale: sometimes the things we chase to escape our pain become the very walls that trap us inside it.*
